metadata.summary: This repository owns the deterministic SDLC enforcement engine published as @agentskit/harness. The Playbook documents practices; the Harness enforces contracts, gates, state transitions, evidence, and recovery.

headings.text: Why files and not a terminal

metadata.summary: A worker's session is opaque: the harness cannot see its model calls, its tool calls or its reasoning. What it can see is a worktree. So the contract between the two is three files, at .ak-loop/ in the worktree root.

headings.text: The rule, and where it is not met yet

metadata.summary: The stages talk to the outside world through three interfaces, chosen by connectors.*:

A contract is the orchestrator's answer to one question: what would make this issue done, and how would anyone know? It is produced once, before dispatch, and frozen — the worker, the review and the merge gate all judge against the same text.

headings.text: The policy orders; it never widens
The ceilings, all of them refusals

metadata.summary: Start with the limit: the loop cannot count what a worker's CLI spends. That session is opaque; its model and tool calls never reach the harness. Everything here is about what the harness itself decides — who it calls, how often, with how much context — plus circuit breakers on signals it can actually observe.

"Done" in an unattended loop has to be decided without a human in the room. One checklist cannot do it: some things are true of every issue in a repository, and some are true only of this one. So there are two lists, and a merge waits for both.

Every transition writes a line to <stateDir>/events.ndjson and emits on the plugin bus. Those events are how debrief, observe, retro and every notification channel know anything: the log is the source of truth, and no report keeps its own state.

metadata.summary: An incident and a refactor of the billing core should not cost the same. A flow profile is how one loop serves both without becoming two loops.

What the loop does without asking

metadata.summary: The loop runs unattended. It stops in exactly these places, and the rule behind all of them is the same: a human decides where the machine would be acting on the world, or acting on itself.
A layer is a slice of the repository with three things attached: the tracker label that places an issue in it, the globs it owns, and the one test that closes it.

headings.text: From a lesson to a memory

metadata.summary: Memory here is not a vector database and not a chat history. It is a small set of approved project decisions that a human (or, within declared bounds, the retro) promoted, recalled into a prompt when they are relevant, and attributed so they can be revoked.

headings.text: Buying the plan without the jury

metadata.summary: With worker.plan.enabled, no worker is launched until a plan has consensus. The planner and the voters run in the harness, headless, before dispatch — the same shape as freezing a contract. The model writes the plan and writes the votes; the machine counts them and decides.

A loop that runs for weeks accumulates evidence about itself. Doing nothing with it wastes it; acting freely on it is how an autonomous system drifts from what its owners agreed to, one defensible step at a time. So the loop may change exactly three things.

A stage is a state machine the harness runs. A model may produce content — a contract, a plan, a vote, a review, an alert triage — but the machine reads that content and decides the transition. That is what makes a run reproducible: the same state produces the same decision, and the event log says which path it took.
Every stage is a machine. A model may write the content a transition reads; the machine reads it and decides. These are the eight.
One person runs the loop on several repositories; one repository is run by several people, on machines that differ. Four files, merged in order and validated once, as one config:
Four roles pick from their own list: orchestrator, reviewer, builder, watcher. Each list is tiers, best first, and every tier is a set of provider/model references.

loop init writes loop.config.yaml from a preset, and a preset is a set of defaults, not a template to fill in. Everything the preset already says is left out of the file it writes, so the config diff a reviewer reads shows what this project decided differently — and nothing else.

headings.text: Install reconciles; it does not rewrite
Drift is invisible to everything else

metadata.summary: Each one runs exactly ak-harness loop stage <x> -f <config> and nothing else. The work happens inside the scheduler's precheck command, which always exits 1 so the run is recorded without launching an agent session. That is runner: precheck, the default, and it is why the loop needs no agent to run itself.
Ten minutes, four commands, nothing irreversible until the last one.

headings.text: What never changes, in any of them

metadata.summary: One motor, three kinds of demand. The issue is the same in all three: the /usage endpoint returns stale counters after a plan change.

headings.text: A plugin, when configuration is not enough

metadata.summary: Three ways to wire the loop into a setup it did not come with. None of them needs a fork.
An unattended loop is judged by how it stops. These are the four ways, in the order they happen to a real project.
The first issue decides what you learn. Pick one that is small, provable and boring — the loop's failure modes are much easier to see when the work itself is not interesting.

headings.text: What the harness will not do

metadata.summary: The contract is frozen. The orchestrator reads the issue and produces a contract: intent, scope, outcomes, and for each outcome the check that proves it. An issue with no verifiable acceptance criterion comes back with zero executable outcomes and one blocking ambiguity — which escalates to a human instead of dispatching a worker to guess.
The package exposes two binaries: ak-harness (everything) and ak-verify (the same binary under the common verification-protocol name). Node.js 22 or newer.
Four commands, in order. Each one is safe to run again, and nothing before the last touches your repository, your tracker or your schedule.

headings.text: Code is a perfectly good agent

metadata.summary: A role can run on a provider alone, or on an agent the project installed — a directory of code and instructions that npx agentskit add <id> copies into the repository.

metadata.summary: loop plan is built to be driven by an agent talking to a person. The machine asks one question at a time and decides when the interview is over; the person answers.

metadata.summary: The harness already aggregates run history, but a benchmark comparison is only meaningful when the baseline is real, attributable, and tied to the same task identity. Manual JSON editing is easy to get wrong and makes the measurement process hard to reproduce.

metadata.title: ADR-0013: Require completed evidence for benchmark comparability

headings.text: ADR-0013: Require completed evidence for benchmark comparability

metadata.summary: An explicit baseline is necessary but not sufficient for a meaningful comparison. A blocked or still-running harness attempt must not be presented as an achieved result, and aggregate pass rates alone do not explain why a task is or is not comparable.

metadata.title: ADR-0014: Criterion-level benchmark evidence
metadata.summary: Scalar baseline numbers do not prove that a benchmark task exercised its acceptance criteria. Treating those numbers as comparable can make an incomplete delivery look like an improvement.

metadata.title: ADR-0015: Directional benchmark outcomes
metadata.summary: The harness already reports raw deltas, but a negative duration delta is easy to misread and non-comparable tasks can be mistaken for missing data. Operators need a small, explicit interpretation layer for the measured resources.

metadata.title: ADR-0016: Baseline evidence digests
metadata.summary: Criterion coverage and directional metrics can still be detached from the exact JSON input used during baseline collection. Without a digest, a later review cannot distinguish the recorded evidence file from a changed copy.
